records.source: חֲז֖וֹן עֹֽבַדְיָ֑ה כֹּֽה־אָמַר֩ אֲדֹנָ֨י יְהוִ֜ה לֶאֱד֗וֹם שְׁמוּעָ֨ה שָׁמַ֜עְנוּ מֵאֵ֤ת יְהוָה֙ וְצִיר֙ בַּגּוֹיִ֣ם שֻׁלָּ֔ח ק֛וּמוּ וְנָק֥וּמָה עָלֶיהָלַמִּלְחָמָֽה׃
records.gloss: Vision of Obadiah. Thus says [the] Lord Yahweh concerning Edom: A report we have heard from with Yahweh, and an envoy among the nations has been sent: Rise up, and let us rise up against her for battle!
pieces: The vision of Obadiah. \q The Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} says this about Edom: We have heard news from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; a messenger has been sent among the nations: \q "Rise up! Let us rise up against her in battle!"

L.1: The vision of Obadiah. \q Thus says the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} concerning Edom: We have heard a report from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and an envoy has been sent among the nations: \q "Rise up, and let us rise up against her for battle!"

R.1: This is the vision that Obadiah saw. \q This is what the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} says about Edom: A message has come to us from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. A messenger has been sent to the nations to say, \q "Get up! Let us go and attack Edom!"

decisions.choice: the vision of Obadiah: the title of the book, naming the prophet and what he received
decisions.reason: "Vision" is the word that heads Isaiah (1:1) and Nahum (1:1): a message the prophet received from God, not only a sight he saw. The name Obadiah means "servant of the LORD" and was common (1 Kings 18:3; Ezra 8:9). Nothing else is known of this prophet, and the book gives no date. Verses 11-14 describe Edom standing by when foreigners entered Jerusalem; this is usually taken to be the fall of the city to Babylon in 586 BC (Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22), which would place the book soon after it. The book does not say so itself.

decisions.choice: verses 1-9 share much of their wording with Jeremiah 49:9-16; this verse is Jeremiah 49:14
decisions.reason: The same report, the envoy sent among the nations and the call to battle against Edom stand in Jeremiah's oracle on Edom (49:14). The wording is reused here where the Hebrew is the same. The differences: Jeremiah says "I have heard", Obadiah "we have heard", joining the prophet with the people who hear the news; and the envoy's call is shorter here, "Rise up, and let us rise up against her", where Jeremiah has "Gather together and come against her, and rise up for battle". Which prophet drew on the other, or whether both drew on an older oracle, cannot be known.

decisions.choice: the envoy's words: the nations call one another to war against Edom
decisions.reason: The envoy is a messenger sent by the LORD among the nations. The words in quotation marks are his summons, and "let us rise up" makes the nations speak with one voice. "Her" is Edom, spoken of as a woman, as lands and cities often are in the prophets. So the LORD is gathering the nations against Edom, though they do not know it.

decisions.choice: Thus says the Lord GOD (L); The Lord GOD says this (B); This is what the Lord GOD says (R)
decisions.reason: The formula as set for the prophets, with the divine name after "Lord" as "the Lord GOD". Literal and Balanced reuse the wording of Jeremiah 49:14 for the rest of the verse; Balanced keeps "Rise up" twice, as the Hebrew does. Readable keeps Jeremiah's "A messenger has been sent to the nations to say", names Edom for "her", and turns "for battle" into "attack". The envoy's call takes double quotation marks as speech quoted inside the oracle.

records.heading: Edom brought down

records.source: הִנֵּ֥ה קָטֹ֛ן נְתַתִּ֖יךָ בַּגּוֹיִ֑ם בָּז֥וּי אַתָּ֖ה מְאֹֽד׃
records.gloss: Look, small I have made you among the nations; despised [are] you exceedingly.
pieces: See, I will make you small among the nations; \q you will be utterly despised.

L.2: Look, I have made you small among the nations; \q you are utterly despised.

R.2: I will make you weak and unimportant among the nations. \q Everyone will look down on you with scorn.

decisions.choice: small among the nations, despised: as Jeremiah 49:15
decisions.reason: Jeremiah 49:15 has the same first line. Its second line reads "despised among humankind"; here it is "you are utterly despised". Jeremiah's verse also begins with "for", which Obadiah lacks.

decisions.choice: I have made you small: the completed form for what God will surely do
alternatives: Edom has already been made small
decisions.reason: The verb has the form used for completed action, but the verses that follow speak of Edom's fall as still to come (verses 4, 8). The prophets often use this form for what God has decided and will surely do, as in Jeremiah 49:15. The same holds for the completed forms in verses 5-7.

decisions.choice: I will make (B, R); utterly despised (L, B); look down on you with scorn (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable reuse the wording of Jeremiah 49:15 and say "I will make" for the completed form (m2). Readable makes "despised" plain and keeps the force of "utterly" with "with scorn".

records.source: זְד֤וֹן לִבְּךָ֙ הִשִּׁיאֶ֔ךָ שֹׁכְנִ֥י בְחַגְוֵי־סֶּ֖לַע מְר֣וֹם שִׁבְתּ֑וֹ אֹמֵ֣ר בְּלִבּ֔וֹ מִ֥י יוֹרִדֵ֖נִי אָֽרֶץ׃
records.gloss: [The] presumption of your heart has deceived you, [you] dwelling in [the] clefts of [the] rock, [the] height his dwelling, saying in his heart, Who will bring me down [to the] ground?
pieces: The pride of your heart has deceived you, \q you who live in the clefts of the rock, whose home is on the heights, \q who say to yourself, \q "Who can bring me down to the ground?"

L.3: The arrogance of your heart has deceived you, \q you dweller in the clefts of the rock, [whose] dwelling [is] on the height, \q who say in [your] heart, \q "Who will bring me down to the ground?"

R.3: Your pride has fooled you. \q You live in hiding places in the rocky cliffs, and your home is high up. \q You say to yourself, \q "No one can bring me down to the ground!"

decisions.choice: the pride that deceives, the clefts of the rock: as Jeremiah 49:16
decisions.reason: Jeremiah 49:16 begins "The terror you cause has deceived you, the arrogance of your heart, you who dwell in the clefts of the rock, who hold the height of the hill". Obadiah has only the arrogance of the heart, and in place of the height of the hill it has "the height of his dwelling", followed by Edom's boast, which Jeremiah lacks.

decisions.choice: the clefts of the rock: Edom's rocky heights
alternatives: the city of Sela
decisions.reason: Edom was a land of steep red sandstone mountains, cut by gorges, with towns built high among the cliffs, hard for an army to reach. The word for "rock" is also the name of an Edomite stronghold, Sela (2 Kings 14:7), so a reader may hear the name in it. As in Jeremiah 49:16, the word is taken as the rock country itself.

decisions.choice: his dwelling ... in his heart: the poem moves from "you" to "he" and back, still speaking of Edom
decisions.reason: The Hebrew addresses Edom as "you", then says "the height of his dwelling" and "who says in his heart", and then returns to "you" in verse 4. Such shifts of person are common in Hebrew poetry and do not change who is meant. Edom's boast is a question that expects the answer "no one"; verse 4 gives God's answer.

decisions.choice: [whose] dwelling ... in [your] heart (L); your (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the words that join the phrases and keeps the change to "his" visible by leaving the pronoun out rather than switching it. Balanced and Readable say "your" throughout, which is what the shift means (m3). Literal and Balanced reuse "has deceived you" and "the clefts of the rock" from Jeremiah 49:16; Readable reuses its "hiding places in the rocky cliffs" and turns the boast into a statement, which is what the question means.

records.source: אִם־תַּגְבִּ֣יהַּ כַּנֶּ֔שֶׁר וְאִם־בֵּ֥ין כּֽוֹכָבִ֖ים שִׂ֣ים קִנֶּ֑ךָ מִשָּׁ֥ם אוֹרִֽידְךָ֖ נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: If you make high like the eagle, and if between [the] stars [is] set your nest, from there I will bring you down, declaration of Yahweh.
pieces: Though you soar as high as the eagle, \q though your nest is placed among the stars, \q I will bring you down from there, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.4: Though you make [it] high like the eagle, \q and though your nest is set among the stars, \q from there I will bring you down, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.4: Even if you fly as high as an eagle \q and build your home among the stars, \q I will bring you down from there, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: the eagle's nest and "from there I will bring you down": as Jeremiah 49:16
decisions.reason: Jeremiah 49:16 ends "Though you make your nest as high as the eagle, from there I will bring you down, declares the LORD." Obadiah adds a second line, "and though your nest is set among the stars", which raises the boast as high as it can go. God answers Edom's question in verse 3: he will bring Edom down.

decisions.choice: make high ... is set: the first verb has no object stated, the second is passive
alternatives: you set your nest among the stars
decisions.reason: "Make high" stands without an object; "your nest" may belong to both lines, or the first may mean "soar". The second verb is passive, "is set". Some read it as an active form, "you set", without change of sense.

decisions.choice: among the stars: as high as can be imagined
decisions.reason: The picture is of pride that reaches to the heavens, as in Isaiah 14:13-15, where the king of Babylon says he will raise his throne above the stars of God and is brought down to Sheol.

decisions.choice: make [it] high (L); soar (B); fly (R); build your home (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the verb with its object supplied in brackets. Balanced and Readable say "soar" and "fly" for an eagle making itself high. Readable says "build your home" for "set your nest", as Jeremiah 49:16 does at that level, and reuses that verse's last line.

records.source: אִם־גַּנָּבִ֤ים בָּאֽוּ־לְךָ֙ אִם־שׁ֣וֹדְדֵי לַ֔יְלָה אֵ֣יךְ נִדְמֵ֔יתָה הֲל֥וֹא יִגְנְב֖וּ דַּיָּ֑ם אִם־בֹּֽצְרִים֙ בָּ֣אוּ לָ֔ךְ הֲל֖וֹא יַשְׁאִ֥ירוּ עֹלֵלֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: If thieves came to you, if destroyers of [the] night, how you are destroyed! Would they not steal their sufficiency? If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave gleanings?
pieces: If thieves came to you, if robbers came by night \q (how you will be destroyed!), \q would they not steal only as much as they wanted? \q If grape pickers came to you, \q would they not leave a few grapes behind?

L.5: If thieves came to you, if plunderers by night \q (how you have been destroyed!), \q would they not steal [only] what was enough for them? \q If grape gatherers came to you, \q would they not leave gleanings?

R.5: When thieves come at night, \q they take only what they want. \q When people pick grapes, \q they leave a few grapes behind. \q But you will be completely destroyed!

decisions.choice: the thieves and the grape gatherers: words shared with Jeremiah 49:9
decisions.reason: Jeremiah 49:9 has the same two pictures in the other order, grape gatherers first. Obadiah puts the thieves first, adds "plunderers" beside them, and breaks into the comparison with a cry, "how you have been destroyed!" In Jeremiah the thieves "destroy" what is enough for them; here they "steal" it.

decisions.choice: would they not ... ? Questions that expect "yes": even thieves and harvesters leave something, but Edom's destroyers will leave nothing
decisions.reason: A thief takes what he wants and leaves the rest; pickers leave gleanings on the vine. The cry in the middle of the verse gives the point: Edom will not be treated even that well. Its ruin will be complete (verse 6).

decisions.choice: gleanings: the few grapes left on the vine after the harvest
decisions.reason: The law told harvesters to leave what they missed for the poor and the foreigner (Leviticus 19:10; Deuteronomy 24:21). Even a full harvest left something behind, as in Jeremiah 49:9.

decisions.choice: how you have been destroyed (L); how you will be destroyed (B); But you will be completely destroyed! (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the completed form; Balanced says "will be", as in verse 2 (see the note there). The cry interrupts the sentence, so Literal and Balanced put it in parentheses. Readable states the two pictures first, as Jeremiah 49:9 does at that level, and then says the point plainly in a sentence of its own at the end; "completely" draws out what the questions imply (m2).

records.source: אֵ֚יךְ נֶחְפְּשׂ֣וּ עֵשָׂ֔ו נִבְע֖וּ מַצְפֻּנָֽיו׃
records.gloss: How they are searched out, Esau! [How] are sought out his hidden treasures!
pieces: How Esau will be ransacked, \q his hidden treasures hunted down!

L.6: How Esau has been searched through, \q his hidden treasures sought out!

R.6: Esau will be robbed of everything! \q Even his hidden treasures will be found and taken!

decisions.choice: Esau: Edom, the people descended from Esau, and Mount Esau, their mountain country
decisions.reason: Esau, Jacob's twin brother, was the ancestor of the Edomites (Genesis 25:24-30; 36:1, 8-9). So the prophets can call the people "Esau", as Jeremiah 49:8-10 does, and Obadiah uses the names Edom, Esau, the house of Esau and Mount Esau for the same people and land. Mount Esau is the mountain country of Seir, south and east of the Dead Sea, which God gave to Esau (Deuteronomy 2:5). The name Esau keeps the story of the two brothers before the reader: the charge in verses 10-14 is that Edom turned on its brother Jacob.

decisions.choice: searched through, his hidden treasures sought out: close to Jeremiah 49:10
decisions.reason: Jeremiah 49:10 says "I have stripped Esau bare; I have uncovered his hiding places". Obadiah uses other verbs, of searching a place thoroughly, and speaks of treasures rather than hiding places. In Jeremiah God acts; here the verbs are passive, and the plunderers of verse 5 do the searching.

decisions.choice: how Esau has been searched: an exclamation, with a plural verb for the people
decisions.reason: "How" opens a cry, as in verse 5. The first verb is plural, because Esau stands for the people of Edom, while "his hidden treasures" treats Esau as one person. The completed form is read as in verse 2.

decisions.choice: searched through ... sought out (L); ransacked ... hunted down (B); robbed of everything ... found and taken (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable choose verbs that make the picture of looters going through every hiding place plain. Every level keeps the name Esau (m1). Balanced and Readable say "will be", as in verse 2.

records.source: עַֽד־הַגְּב֣וּל שִׁלְּח֗וּךָ כֹּ֚ל אַנְשֵׁ֣י בְרִיתֶ֔ךָ הִשִּׁיא֛וּךָ יָכְל֥וּ לְךָ֖ אַנְשֵׁ֣י שְׁלֹמֶ֑ךָ לַחְמְךָ֗ יָשִׂ֤ימוּ מָזוֹר֙ תַּחְתֶּ֔יךָ אֵ֥ין תְּבוּנָ֖ה בּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: To the border they have sent you, all [the] men of your covenant; they have deceived you, they have prevailed against you, [the] men of your peace; your bread they set [as] a trap under you; there is no understanding in him.
pieces: All your allies will drive you to the border; \q your friends will deceive you and overpower you; \q those who share your bread will lay a trap for you. \q There is no understanding in Edom.

L.7: To the border they have sent you, all the men of your covenant; \q they have deceived you, they have overpowered you, the men of your peace; \q [those who eat] your bread set a trap under you; \q there is no understanding in him.

R.7: All your allies will chase you out to the border. \q Your friends will trick you and defeat you. \q The people who eat at your table will set a trap for you. \q And Edom will not understand.

decisions.choice: the men of your covenant ... the men of your peace: Edom's allies and friends
decisions.reason: A covenant here is a treaty between nations. "The men of your peace" are those at peace with Edom, its friends (Psalm 41:10; Jeremiah 38:22). The verse does not name them; nearby peoples such as the Arabian tribes are often suggested. The point is that Edom will be betrayed by those it trusted, as it betrayed its brother.

decisions.choice: your bread ... a trap: those who share your bread will set a trap for you
alternatives: they will set your bread as a trap
they will place a wound under you
decisions.reason: The line is hard. It says "your bread they set a trap under you". It is taken here as short for "those who eat your bread", the friends who share Edom's table (Psalm 41:10 speaks of a friend "who ate my bread" turning against the speaker). The word rendered "trap" is rare; it may mean a snare or net, and elsewhere a word spelled the same way means a wound or sore (Hosea 5:13). Some ancient translations differ here; the sense of betrayal by friends is clear either way.

decisions.choice: there is no understanding in him: Edom, famed for its wisdom, does not see what is happening
alternatives: there is no understanding of it (the trap)
decisions.reason: "Him" is Edom (as in verse 3), and the line leads into verse 8, where God removes understanding from Mount Esau. Read the other way, the phrase means that the trap is set without Edom's knowing it. Both readings say that Edom is caught unawares.

decisions.choice: they have sent you ... deceived you ... overpowered you: completed forms for what will surely happen
decisions.reason: As in verse 2, the completed forms describe what God has decided. Edom's own allies will push it out to its borders, perhaps as refugees or as envoys sent away empty-handed.

decisions.choice: [those who eat] your bread (L); those who eat your bread (B); the people who eat at your table (R); Edom (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the words supplied to make the line read (m2); Balanced and Readable state them. Balanced and Readable name Edom for "him" so the reader is not lost, and use "will" for the completed forms (m4). Readable says "chase you out" for "send you to the border".

records.source: הֲל֛וֹא בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה וְהַאֲבַדְתִּ֤י חֲכָמִים֙ מֵֽאֱד֔וֹם וּתְבוּנָ֖ה מֵהַ֥ר עֵשָֽׂו׃
records.gloss: Will I not on that day, declaration of Yahweh, destroy [the] wise from Edom and understanding from [the] mountain of Esau?
pieces: On that day, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q will I not destroy the wise from Edom, \q and understanding from Mount Esau?

L.8: Will I not on that day, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q destroy the wise from Edom, \q and understanding from Mount Esau?

R.8: On that day, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q I will destroy the wise people of Edom. \q No understanding will be left on Mount Esau.

decisions.choice: the wise of Edom: Edom was known for its wisdom
decisions.reason: Jeremiah's oracle on Edom opens "Is there no more wisdom in Teman?" (49:7), and Job's friend Eliphaz, the wisest of them, came from Teman in Edom (Job 2:11). The verse uses Edom's pride in its wisdom against it: the understanding it lacks in verse 7 will be taken away altogether.

decisions.choice: will I not ... ? A question that expects "yes"
decisions.reason: The question is a strong statement: on that day God will certainly do it. "That day" is the day of Edom's judgment, which verse 15 joins to the day of the LORD on all the nations.

decisions.choice: On that day, declares the LORD, will I not ... (B); I will destroy (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced puts "on that day" first, where English expects it. Readable states the question as the promise it is (m2) and makes the second line a sentence of its own.

records.source: וְחַתּ֥וּ גִבּוֹרֶ֖יךָ תֵּימָ֑ן לְמַ֧עַן יִכָּֽרֶת־אִ֛ישׁ מֵהַ֥ר עֵשָׂ֖ו מִקָּֽטֶל׃
records.gloss: And will be dismayed your mighty men, Teman, so that will be cut off everyone from [the] mountain of Esau by slaughter.
pieces: Your warriors will be terrified, Teman, \q so that everyone on Mount Esau will be cut down in the slaughter.

L.9: And your mighty men will be shattered, Teman, \q so that everyone will be cut off from Mount Esau by slaughter.

R.9: Your soldiers, Teman, will be terrified, \q and everyone on Mount Esau will be killed.

decisions.choice: Teman: one of Edom's chief regions, standing for the whole land
decisions.reason: Teman was a region, and perhaps a town, in the south of Edom, named after a grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:11). As in Jeremiah 49:7 and 20, it stands for Edom as a whole, beside Mount Esau.

decisions.choice: by slaughter: the last words of verse 9
alternatives: the first words of verse 10: "because of the slaughter, because of the violence done to your brother Jacob"
decisions.reason: The verse division and the accents of the Hebrew text place "by slaughter" at the end of verse 9. Some ancient translations, among them the Greek and the Latin, join it to verse 10, so that Edom is judged "because of the slaughter" of its brother. The Hebrew division is followed. This description of the ancient translations is written from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: dismayed: shattered with terror
decisions.reason: The verb means to be broken, and so to be broken in spirit, terrified (Jeremiah 49:37). The warriors lose their nerve, and the people are left without defense.

decisions.choice: shattered (L); terrified (B, R); cut down ... killed (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the picture of breaking; Balanced and Readable give its sense here, terror. "Everyone" is the Hebrew "each man"; the sense is everyone left on Mount Esau. Readable says "killed" for "cut off by slaughter".

records.source: מֵחֲמַ֛ס אָחִ֥יךָ יַעֲקֹ֖ב תְּכַסְּךָ֣ בוּשָׁ֑ה וְנִכְרַ֖תָּ לְעוֹלָֽם׃
records.gloss: Because of [the] violence [to] your brother Jacob, shame will cover you, and you will be cut off forever.
pieces: Because of the violence you did to your brother Jacob, \q you will be covered in shame and cut off forever.

L.10: Because of the violence [done to] your brother Jacob, disgrace will cover you, \q and you will be cut off for all time.

R.10: You were cruel to your brother Jacob's people, so you will be covered with shame, \q and you will be destroyed forever.

decisions.choice: your brother Jacob: the charge is that Edom wronged its own brother
decisions.reason: Esau and Jacob were twins (Genesis 25:24-26), and the law reminded Israel that "the Edomite is your brother" (Deuteronomy 23:8; compare Numbers 20:14). Edom's guilt is the greater because the violence was done to its own kin. Here the verses turn from Edom's pride to the reason for its judgment, set out in verses 11-14.

decisions.choice: violence: wrong done by force, cruelty
decisions.reason: The word means violent wrongdoing, the cruelty that breaks the bonds between people (Genesis 6:11; Joel 4:19, where it is again used of Edom's violence against Judah).

decisions.choice: [done to] (L); you did to (B); You were cruel to your brother Jacob's people (R); disgrace (L); shame (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "the violence of your brother", meaning the violence done to him. Literal brackets the words that say so; Balanced and Readable state them. Readable says "Jacob's people" because Jacob here stands for the nation descended from him, and "destroyed" for "cut off". Literal says "disgrace" and "for all time", Balanced and Readable "shame" and "forever"; the words mean the same.

records.source: בְּיוֹם֙ עֲמָֽדְךָ֣ מִנֶּ֔גֶד בְּי֛וֹם שְׁב֥וֹת זָרִ֖ים חֵיל֑וֹ וְנָכְרִ֞ים בָּ֣אוּ שְׁעָרָ֗יו וְעַל־יְרוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ יַדּ֣וּ גוֹרָ֔ל גַּם־אַתָּ֖ה כְּאַחַ֥ד מֵהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: On [the] day you stood aloof, on [the] day strangers carried off his wealth, and foreigners entered his gates, and for Jerusalem they cast lots, also you [were] like one of them.
pieces: On the day you stood at a distance, \q on the day strangers carried off his wealth \q and foreigners entered his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem, \q you were like one of them.

L.11: On the day you stood aloof, \q on the day strangers carried off his wealth, \q and foreigners entered his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem, \q you too [were] like one of them.

R.11: You stood by and watched \q when strangers carried off your brother's wealth. \q Foreigners came through his gates and threw lots to divide up Jerusalem. \q You were just like them!

decisions.choice: the day strangers entered Jerusalem: the fall of the city, usually taken to be the Babylonian conquest of 586 BC
alternatives: an earlier attack on Jerusalem, such as that of the Philistines and Arabians in the days of Jehoram (2 Chronicles 21:16-17)
decisions.reason: The verse does not name the enemy. Psalm 137:7 remembers the Edomites crying "Tear it down!" on the day Jerusalem fell to Babylon, and Lamentations 4:21-22 and Ezekiel 35:5, 10-15 also accuse Edom over that disaster. That is the usual identification. Jerusalem was attacked more than once, and the description fits other attacks too.

decisions.choice: his wealth: Jacob's goods, or his army
alternatives: his army, carried off into captivity
decisions.reason: The word means strength, and so either wealth or a fighting force. The verb means to take captive. Carrying off goods fits verse 13, where Edom reaches for Jacob's wealth; but the line can also mean that strangers took his army captive.

decisions.choice: cast lots for Jerusalem: divided the city and its people as plunder
decisions.reason: Victors cast lots to share out captured people and goods (Joel 4:3; Nahum 3:10; Psalm 22:19). Edom took no part in the fighting, but by standing by it was like one of the conquerors.

decisions.choice: stood aloof (L); stood at a distance (B); stood by and watched (R)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says that Edom stood "from opposite", at a distance, as an onlooker who will not help. Readable says what that meant. Readable names "your brother" for "his", so the reader can follow who is meant, and says "threw lots to divide up" for casting lots (m3).

records.source: וְאַל־תֵּ֤רֶא בְיוֹם־אָחִ֨יךָ֙ בְּי֣וֹם נָכְר֔וֹ וְאַל־תִּשְׂמַ֥ח לִבְנֵֽי־יְהוּדָ֖ה בְּי֣וֹם אָבְדָ֑ם וְאַל־תַּגְדֵּ֥ל פִּ֖יךָ בְּי֥וֹם צָרָֽה׃
records.gloss: And do not look on [the] day of your brother, on [the] day of his misfortune; and do not rejoice over [the] sons of Judah on [the] day of their perishing; and do not make big your mouth on [the] day of distress.
pieces: You should not have gloated over your brother's day, the day of his misfortune, \q nor rejoiced over the people of Judah on the day of their ruin, \q nor boasted so loudly on the day of their distress.

L.12: But do not look on the day of your brother, on the day of his misfortune; \q do not rejoice over the {{gender:children|sons}} of Judah on the day of their ruin; \q do not make your mouth big on the day of distress.

R.12: You should not have enjoyed watching your brother on the day his trouble came. \q You should not have been glad when the people of Judah were destroyed. \q You should not have bragged on the day they were in distress.

decisions.choice: do not look ... do not rejoice: commands spoken as if the day were still before Edom, condemning what it did
alternatives: warnings against doing these things in a disaster still to come
decisions.reason: Verses 12-14 are a series of eight commands, "do not ...". Verse 11 has already described the day as past, so the commands are taken as the prophet's vivid way of condemning what Edom did: he puts himself on that day and cries out against each act in turn. Some read them as warnings for the future. Either way, they set out what Edom is judged for.

decisions.choice: look on: gaze with pleasure; make your mouth big: boast, mock
decisions.reason: To "look on" someone's day of trouble is to watch it with satisfaction (Psalm 22:18; Micah 7:10). To "make the mouth big" is to speak proudly and mockingly (Ezekiel 35:13, again of Edom).

decisions.choice: the day: the day of disaster, named again and again
decisions.reason: The word "day" comes ten times in verses 11-14. The repetition fixes the reader on the one day of Judah's ruin, and leads to "the day of the LORD" in verse 15, when the day will turn on Edom.

decisions.choice: do not (L); You should not have (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the form of the commands. Balanced and Readable say what they mean here, a condemnation of past acts (m1), with "You should not have". Balanced says "gloated" and "boasted so loudly" for the idioms (m2); Readable says "enjoyed watching" and "bragged".

records.source: אַל־תָּב֤וֹא בְשַֽׁעַר־עַמִּי֙ בְּי֣וֹם אֵידָ֔ם אַל־תֵּ֧רֶא גַם־אַתָּ֛ה בְּרָעָת֖וֹ בְּי֣וֹם אֵיד֑וֹ וְאַל־תִּשְׁלַ֥חְנָה בְחֵיל֖וֹ בְּי֥וֹם אֵידֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: Do not enter into [the] gate of my people on [the] day of their disaster; do not look, also you, on his calamity on [the] day of his disaster; and do not stretch out [a hand] on his wealth on [the] day of his disaster.
pieces: You should not have marched through the gate of my people on the day of their disaster, \q nor gloated, you of all people, over his calamity on the day of his disaster, \q nor seized his wealth on the day of his disaster.

L.13: Do not enter the gate of my people on the day of their disaster; \q do not look, you too, on his calamity on the day of his disaster; \q and do not stretch out [your hand] against his wealth on the day of his disaster.

R.13: You should not have marched through the gates of my people's city on the day disaster struck them. \q You, of all people, should not have enjoyed seeing them suffer on the day of their disaster. \q You should not have taken their wealth on the day of their disaster.

decisions.choice: the day of his disaster, three times: a play on the name Edom
decisions.reason: The word for disaster in these lines sounds like the name Edom, and it comes three times, at the end of each line. The sound ties Edom's name to Judah's ruin, and the reader is left to hear that Edom's own disaster is coming (verse 15).

decisions.choice: my people: the LORD speaks
decisions.reason: The oracle began "Thus says the Lord GOD" (verse 1), and here the speaker calls Judah "my people". Edom's wrong was done to the LORD's own people.

decisions.choice: stretch out: stretch out the hand to seize
decisions.reason: The verb is used without its object, "hand", as it sometimes is (2 Samuel 6:6). Its form is unusual, and some read it as a slip for the usual form "you"; the sense is the same: Edom took part in the looting. "You too" in the second line means "you, of all people", the brother.

decisions.choice: do not (L); You should not have (B, R); disaster (all levels)
decisions.reason: As in verse 12, Balanced and Readable state the commands as condemnation. Every level keeps "disaster" at the end of each line, so the repetition can be heard (m1). Readable says "my people's city" for "the gate of my people", and "them" for "his", since Judah is meant.

records.source: וְאַֽל־תַּעֲמֹד֙ עַל־הַפֶּ֔רֶק לְהַכְרִ֖ית אֶת־פְּלִיטָ֑יו וְאַל־תַּסְגֵּ֥ר שְׂרִידָ֖יו בְּי֥וֹם צָרָֽה׃
records.gloss: And do not stand at the crossing to cut off his fugitives; and do not hand over his survivors on [the] day of distress.
pieces: You should not have stood at the crossroads \q to cut down those who escaped, \q nor handed over his survivors on the day of distress.

L.14: And do not stand at the crossroads \q to cut off his fugitives; \q and do not hand over his survivors on the day of distress.

R.14: You should not have waited where the roads meet to kill those who were running away. \q You should not have handed over the survivors to their enemies on that day of distress.

decisions.choice: the crossroads: a place where the road divides, where fugitives could be stopped
alternatives: a mountain pass
a place to plunder
decisions.reason: The word is rare. It seems to mean a fork or a parting of the ways, where those fleeing Jerusalem would have to pass. Some take it as a narrow pass. Edom waited where the escaping people would come.

decisions.choice: hand over his survivors: deliver them to the enemy
alternatives: shut them in
decisions.reason: The verb means to shut up, and so to hand someone over into another's power (Amos 1:6, 9, where Philistia and Tyre hand over whole communities to Edom). Edom caught the survivors and gave them up to the conquerors.

decisions.choice: You should not have (B, R); to their enemies (R)
decisions.reason: As in verses 12-13, Balanced and Readable state the commands as condemnation. Readable says to whom the survivors were handed over (m2), and "where the roads meet" for the crossroads.

records.source: כִּֽי־קָר֥וֹב יוֹם־יְהוָ֖ה עַל־כָּל־הַגּוֹיִ֑ם כַּאֲשֶׁ֤ר עָשִׂ֨יתָ֙ יֵעָ֣שֶׂה לָּ֔ךְ גְּמֻלְךָ֖ יָשׁ֥וּב בְּרֹאשֶֽׁךָ׃
records.gloss: For near [is the] day of Yahweh on all the nations; as you have done, it will be done to you; your dealing will return on your head.
pieces: For the day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is close at hand for all the nations. \q As you have done, so it will be done to you; \q what you have dealt out will come back on your own head.

L.15: For near [is] the day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} upon all the nations; \q just as you have done, it will be done to you; \q your dealing will return on your own head.

R.15: The day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is near for all the nations. \q What you did to others will be done to you. \q The harm you did will come back on you.

decisions.choice: the day of the LORD: the day when the LORD comes to judge
decisions.reason: The prophets speak of "the day of the LORD" as the time when God acts in judgment, against the nations and against his own people when they sin (Isaiah 13:6; Joel 1:15; Amos 5:18). Here Edom's day of judgment, "that day" of verse 8, becomes part of the LORD's day on all nations. The day Edom watched in verses 11-14 was Judah's; now the day is the LORD's.

decisions.choice: as you have done, it will be done to you: Edom will be repaid in kind
decisions.reason: The punishment matches the crime (compare Jeremiah 50:15, 29; Ezekiel 35:15). "Your dealing" is what Edom did to others, which will come back "on your own head", that is, on Edom itself (Joel 4:4, 7).

decisions.choice: the day of the LORD, at every level
decisions.reason: As set for the prophets, "the day of the LORD" is kept word for word at every level (Isaiah 13:6), so that the reader can follow the phrase through the books. Readable says "on you" for "on your own head".

records.source: כִּ֗י כַּֽאֲשֶׁ֤ר שְׁתִיתֶם֙ עַל־הַ֣ר קָדְשִׁ֔י יִשְׁתּ֥וּ כָֽל־הַגּוֹיִ֖ם תָּמִ֑יד וְשָׁת֣וּ וְלָע֔וּ וְהָי֖וּ כְּל֥וֹא הָיֽוּ׃
records.gloss: For just as you have drunk on my holy mountain, all the nations will drink continually; and they will drink and swallow, and they will be as [if] they had not been.
pieces: Just as you drank on my holy mountain, \q all the nations will keep on drinking; \q they will drink and gulp it down, \q and be as if they had never existed.

L.16: For just as you have drunk on my holy mountain, \q all the nations will drink continually; \q they will drink and gulp down, \q and they will be as though they had never been.

R.16: Just as you drank on my holy mountain, \q all the nations will keep drinking the cup of my anger. \q They will drink it all down, \q and they will disappear as if they had never lived.

decisions.choice: you have drunk: "you" is now plural, and who is meant is not said
alternatives: the people of Judah, who drank the cup of judgment when Jerusalem fell
the Edomites, who drank in celebration on the captured mountain
decisions.reason: Until now Edom has been "you" in the singular; here the verb is plural. Read as Judah, the verse says that as God's own people drank the cup of his anger on Mount Zion, so all the nations will drink it now (Jeremiah 25:28-29; 49:12). Read as Edom, it says that as they caroused on God's mountain after its fall, so the nations will drink the cup of judgment. The Hebrew allows both, and the drinking of the nations is judgment either way.

decisions.choice: the nations will drink: the cup of God's wrath
decisions.reason: The prophets picture judgment as a cup of wine that God makes the nations drink until they stagger and fall (Isaiah 51:17-23; Jeremiah 25:15-29; 49:12, where Edom must drink it; Lamentations 4:21).

decisions.choice: swallow: gulp down
alternatives: talk wildly
stagger
decisions.reason: The verb is rare. It seems to mean gulping down, drinking the cup to the last drop. Some take it as reeling or talking wildly, as drunkards do. In both readings the drinking ends in the nations' disappearance.

decisions.choice: the cup of my anger (R)
decisions.reason: Readable names the cup, which the verse implies (m2), so the reader can see that the drinking is judgment. It keeps "you drank" without saying who "you" are (m1).

records.source: וּבְהַ֥ר צִיּ֛וֹן תִּהְיֶ֥ה פְלֵיטָ֖ה וְהָ֣יָה קֹ֑דֶשׁ וְיָֽרְשׁוּ֙ בֵּ֣ית יַֽעֲקֹ֔ב אֵ֖ת מוֹרָֽשֵׁיהֶם׃
records.gloss: And on Mount Zion will be escape, and it will be holy; and will possess [the] house of Jacob their possessions.
pieces: But on Mount Zion there will be survivors, and it will be holy; \q and the house of Jacob will take possession of what belongs to them.

L.17: But on Mount Zion there will be escape, and it will be holy; \q and the house of Jacob will possess their possessions.

R.17: But on Mount Zion some people will escape, and it will be a holy place. \q The people of Jacob will take back the land that belongs to them.

decisions.choice: escape: a place of escape, and those who escape
decisions.reason: The word means escape and also the people who escape, the survivors. Edom cut off Judah's fugitives (verse 14); now Mount Zion will hold survivors. Joel 3:5 takes up the same words: "on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as the LORD has said".

decisions.choice: it will be holy: Zion will again be the LORD's holy place
decisions.reason: The nations defiled God's holy mountain (verse 16); now it will be holy again, set apart for the LORD, and foreigners will no longer pass through it (Joel 4:17).

decisions.choice: their possessions: the house of Jacob will take back its own land
alternatives: those who dispossessed them
decisions.reason: With different vowels the same letters can be read "those who dispossessed them", so that Jacob takes possession of the peoples who had taken its land. The Greek translation reads it that way. The Hebrew text as written is followed; verses 19-20 describe Israel taking back its own land and more. This description of the Greek is written from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: the land that belongs to them (R)
decisions.reason: The word for possessions is used of an inheritance, especially of land (Deuteronomy 2:5, where the same root describes Esau's own land). Readable says "land" because verses 19-20 show that land is meant, and "take back" because it was theirs.

records.source: וְהָיָה֩ בֵית־יַעֲקֹ֨ב אֵ֜שׁ וּבֵ֧ית יוֹסֵ֣ף לֶהָבָ֗ה וּבֵ֤ית עֵשָׂו֙ לְקַ֔שׁ וְדָלְק֥וּ בָהֶ֖ם וַאֲכָל֑וּם וְלֹֽא־יִֽהְיֶ֤השָׂרִיד֙ לְבֵ֣ית עֵשָׂ֔ו כִּ֥י יְהוָ֖ה דִּבֵּֽר׃
records.gloss: And will be [the] house of Jacob a fire, and [the] house of Joseph a flame, and [the] house of Esau stubble; and they will burn among them and consume them, and there will not be a survivor to [the] house of Esau, for Yahweh has spoken.
pieces: The house of Jacob will become a fire, and the house of Joseph will be a flame, and the house of Esau will be stubble; \q they will set them ablaze and burn them up. \q No survivor will be left to the house of Esau, \q for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has spoken.

L.18: And the house of Jacob will be fire, and the house of Joseph flame, and the house of Esau [will be] stubble; \q they will set them ablaze and consume them, \q and there will be no survivor for the house of Esau, \q for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has spoken.

R.18: Jacob's people will be a fire and Joseph's people a flame, and the house of Esau will be like dry straw. \q Jacob's people will set them on fire and burn them up. \q No one from the house of Esau will survive. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has said this!

decisions.choice: the house of Jacob and the house of Joseph: the whole people of Israel, south and north
decisions.reason: Joseph, the father of Ephraim and Manasseh, stands for the northern tribes (Amos 5:6; Ezekiel 37:16-19). With the house of Jacob beside it, the verse pictures the whole people reunited and acting together against Esau.

decisions.choice: fire, flame and stubble: a picture of swift, complete destruction
decisions.reason: Stubble, the dry stalks left after the harvest, burns at once (Exodus 15:7; Isaiah 5:24; Malachi 3:19). The brother who stood by while Jacob burned is now himself the fuel.

decisions.choice: for the LORD has spoken: the closing seal on the oracle
decisions.reason: The phrase marks a word as certain, because it is the LORD's (Isaiah 1:20; Joel 4:8). "No survivor" answers verse 14, where Edom handed over Judah's survivors.

decisions.choice: stubble (L, B); dry straw (R); survivor
decisions.reason: Readable says "dry straw" for stubble, which may be an unfamiliar word, and makes "they" plain as Jacob's people. Every level keeps "the house of Esau".

records.source: וְיָרְשׁ֨וּ הַנֶּ֜גֶב אֶת־הַ֣ר עֵשָׂ֗ו וְהַשְּׁפֵלָה֙ אֶת־פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וְיָרְשׁוּ֙ אֶת־שְׂדֵ֣ה אֶפְרַ֔יִם וְאֵ֖ת שְׂדֵ֣ה שֹׁמְר֑וֹן וּבִנְיָמִ֖ן אֶת־הַגִּלְעָֽד׃
records.gloss: And they will possess the Negev, [the] mountain of Esau, and the Shephelah, [the] Philistines; and they will possess [the] field of Ephraim and [the] field of Samaria, and Benjamin, the Gilead.
pieces: The people of the Negev will take possession of Mount Esau, and the people of the Shephelah the land of the Philistines; \q they will take possession of the territory of Ephraim \q and the territory of Samaria, \q and Benjamin will possess Gilead.

L.19: And [those of] the Negev will possess Mount Esau, and [those of] the Shephelah the Philistines; \q and they will possess the territory of Ephraim \q and the territory of Samaria, \q and Benjamin [will possess] Gilead.

R.19: People from the Negev desert in the south will take over Mount Esau. People from the western foothills will take over the land of the Philistines. \q They will take over the land of Ephraim \q and the land of Samaria. \q The people of Benjamin will take over Gilead.

decisions.choice: those of the Negev will possess Mount Esau: each region of Judah takes the land beside it
alternatives: they will possess the Negev and Mount Esau, the Shephelah and the Philistines
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is brief. "The Negev" and "the Shephelah" have no marker of the object, while "Mount Esau" and "the Philistines" do, so the first of each pair is taken as the people who will possess the second: the people of the Negev, Judah's southern desert, take Edom's mountains to the south-east, and the people of the Shephelah, the low hills to the west, take the Philistine plain. Read the other way, "they", the house of Jacob of verse 18, take all four. The picture is the same: the land is restored and enlarged on every side.

decisions.choice: Ephraim, Samaria, Benjamin and Gilead: the lands of the north and east
decisions.reason: Ephraim and Samaria were the heart of the northern kingdom, lost to Assyria in 722 BC. Benjamin lay just north of Jerusalem, and Gilead was Israel's land east of the Jordan. The verse pictures the whole land of Israel restored to its people.

decisions.choice: [those of] (L); the people of (B, R); the western foothills (R); the land of (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the words that show the reading taken (m1); Balanced and Readable state them. Readable explains the Negev and the Shephelah by where they lay, as Jeremiah 17:26 does at that level. "Territory" is the Hebrew "field", a stretch of land.

records.source: וְגָלֻ֣ת הַֽחֵל־הַ֠זֶּה לִבְנֵ֨י יִשְׂרָאֵ֤ל אֲשֶֽׁר־כְּנַעֲנִים֙ עַד־צָ֣רְפַ֔ת וְגָלֻ֥ת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם אֲשֶׁ֣ר בִּסְפָרַ֑ד יִֽרְשׁ֕וּ אֵ֖ת עָרֵ֥י הַנֶּֽגֶב׃
records.gloss: And [the] exiles of this host of [the] sons of Israel, which [is] Canaanites as far as Zarephath, and [the] exiles of Jerusalem who [are] in Sepharad will possess [the] cities of the Negev.
pieces: The exiles of this army of Israel will take possession of the Canaanite land as far as Zarephath, \q and the exiles of Jerusalem who are in Sepharad \q will possess the towns of the Negev.

L.20: And the exiles of this host of the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel [will possess] what [belongs to] the Canaanites as far as Zarephath; \q and the exiles of Jerusalem who [are] in Sepharad \q will take possession of the cities of the Negev.

R.20: This large group of Israel's people who were taken away as prisoners will take over the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath. \q And the people from Jerusalem who were taken away to Sepharad \q will take over the towns of the Negev.

decisions.choice: the exiles of Israel will possess the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath
alternatives: the exiles of Israel who are among the Canaanites as far as Zarephath, together with the exiles of Jerusalem, will possess the cities of the Negev
decisions.reason: This is the hardest verse in the book. It reads word for word "and the exiles of this host of the sons of Israel which Canaanites as far as Zarephath". It is taken here as a clause whose verb, "will possess", is understood from the end of the verse: the exiles of the north take the coast as far as Zarephath, and the exiles of Jerusalem take the Negev. It can also be read as one long subject, the exiles living among the Canaanites, so that both groups of exiles return to the cities of the Negev. "Host" may mean an army or a large company; some take it as a fortress or as a place name.

decisions.choice: the Canaanites as far as Zarephath: the Phoenician coast to the north
decisions.reason: Zarephath was a town on the coast between Tyre and Sidon, where Elijah stayed with a widow (1 Kings 17:9). "Canaanites" here means the Phoenicians of that coast.

decisions.choice: Sepharad: a place of exile not known for certain
alternatives: Sardis in Asia Minor
a place in Media or elsewhere in the east
decisions.reason: Sepharad is named only here. It is often identified with Sardis, the capital of Lydia in Asia Minor, whose name is written in a similar way in old inscriptions; others suggest places in the east. Later Jewish tradition took it to mean Spain, and the Jews of Spain and their descendants are still called Sephardim from this verse. The text says only that some of Jerusalem's exiles were there.

decisions.choice: [will possess] what [belongs to] (L); this large group ... taken away as prisoners (R)
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the words that the reading in m1 supplies; Balanced states them. Readable explains "exiles" as people taken away as prisoners and gives "host" as a large group, without choosing between army and company.

records.source: וְעָל֤וּ מֽוֹשִׁעִים֙ בְּהַ֣ר צִיּ֔וֹן לִשְׁפֹּ֖ט אֶת־הַ֣ר עֵשָׂ֑ו וְהָיְתָ֥ה לַֽיהוָ֖ה הַמְּלוּכָֽה׃
records.gloss: And will go up deliverers on Mount Zion to judge [the] mountain of Esau, and will be to Yahweh the kingship.
pieces: Deliverers will go up onto Mount Zion \q to rule over Mount Esau, \q and the kingdom will belong to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.21: And deliverers will go up on Mount Zion \q to judge Mount Esau, \q and the kingship will belong to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.21: Leaders who rescue God's people will go up onto Mount Zion \q to rule over Mount Esau. \q And the kingdom will belong to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: deliverers: leaders who save the people, like the judges
alternatives: those who have been delivered
decisions.reason: The word is used of the leaders God raised up in the book of Judges to rescue Israel (Judges 3:9, 15; Nehemiah 9:27). The Greek translation reads it with other vowels as "those who have been delivered", the rescued people themselves. The Hebrew text is followed. This description of the Greek is written from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: to judge: to rule and to bring justice
alternatives: to punish
decisions.reason: The verb means to judge, and so to govern, as the judges of Israel did. Mount Esau, which looked down on Jerusalem (verse 3), will be ruled from Mount Zion. The two mountains frame the end of the book.

decisions.choice: the kingship will belong to the LORD: the book's last word
decisions.reason: The book ends not with Israel's victory but with the LORD's reign. The deliverers rule under him, and the kingdom is his (Psalm 22:29; Zechariah 14:9).

decisions.choice: deliverers (L, B); leaders who rescue God's people (R); judge (L); rule over (B, R); kingship (L); kingdom (B, R)
decisions.reason: Readable explains "deliverers" (m1). Balanced and Readable say "rule over" for the sense of "judge" here (m2), and "kingdom" for the reign that belongs to the LORD.
